sec: Portal hypertension: clinical significance and pathogenesis · p1001

items.q: ‘Portal hypertension occurs only in the presence of cirrhosis.’
opts: False — it can manifest with or without cirrhosis
True — cirrhosis is a mandatory prerequisite
False — it occurs exclusively without cirrhosis
True, but only in post-hepatic forms
items.exp: Opening line of the chapter: portal hypertension can manifest with or without cirrhosis. (Book p1001)

items.q: Match the p1001 outcome chains — 1) Portal hypertension  2) Ascites  3) Jaundice + liver failure  4) Raised splenic pressure … A) Average survival without transplant printed as ‘a years’  B) Leads to hepatorenal syndrome  C) Hepatic encephalopathy and variceal bleeding  D) Splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia
items.exp: Portal hypertension leads to hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding and ascites; ascites (1st sign of decompensation) leads to hepatorenal syndrome; jaundice + liver failure = decompensation with average survival ‘a years’ without transplant as printed; raised splenic pressure gives splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia. (Book p1001)

items.q: The 1st sign of decompensation in portal hypertension is:
items.exp: Under the bullet ‘ascites’ the page states ‘1st sign of decompensation’. (Book p1001)

items.q: Portal hypertension is defined by a portal venous pressure of:
items.exp: Pathogenesis line: portal venous pressure ≥ 12 mm Hg. (Book p1001)

items.q: Sinusoidal pressure is defined as ≥ 6 mm Hg; it becomes clinically significant at:
items.exp: ‘Sinusoidal pressure ≥ 6 mm Hg (clinically significant if ≥ 10 mm Hg)’. (Book p1001)

items.q: A 48-year-old with biopsy-proven cirrhosis has a spleen 4 cm below the costal margin and a platelet count of 90,000/µL. Which pair gives the earliest clinical and earliest biochemical manifestations of portal hypertension?
items.exp: Raised splenic pressure → splenomegaly (earliest clinical) and thrombocytopenia (earliest biochemical). (Book p1001)

items.q: The mean survival without decompensation or transplant in portal hypertension is:
items.exp: ‘Mean survival without decompensation / transplant : 12 years’. (Book p1001)

items.q: After decompensation (jaundice + liver failure), average survival without transplant is about:
items.exp: The page prints ‘Decompensation : Average survival a years without transplant’ — the ‘a’ is a typographical slip for 1, i.e. about 1 year, in contrast to the 12 years without decompensation. (Book p1001)

items.q: All but one of the following are listed under ‘Portal hypertension leads to’. The odd one out is:
items.exp: The three listed consequences are hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding and ascites; hepatomegaly is not listed. (Book p1001)

items.q: ‘Thrombocytopenia is the earliest clinical manifestation of portal hypertension.’
opts: False — splenomegaly is the earliest clinical, thrombocytopenia the earliest biochemical
True — thrombocytopenia is the earliest clinical manifestation of portal hypertension
False — both findings are biochemical rather than clinical manifestations
True — but only when splenic vein thrombosis is present alongside cirrhosis
items.exp: Raised splenic pressure → splenomegaly (earliest clinical) and thrombocytopenia (earliest biochemical). (Book p1001)
